script.opening: (A bit embarrassed; casual tone, keen to play it down.) "Hi doc. This is a bit embarrassing — I keep waking up absolutely drenched in sweat, soaking the sheets, most nights for over a month. It's probably just stress, work's been mad, or maybe my room's too warm. Could you give me something to help me sleep, or is it just one of those things? I'm sure it's nothing serious."

facts.text: About six weeks, most nights. "Yes, sometimes twice a night" — has to change his T-shirt and the sheets. Room temperature hasn't changed. No hot flushes during the day.
If asked: "Yeah, actually. My clothes are looser. I thought it was the stress." About 5 kg (nearly a stone) over two months without trying.
"I haven't measured a temperature." Feels hot and shivery some evenings. If asked about itch: "I've been really itchy, all over, for a few weeks" — no rash.

facts.topic: The lump — only if asked about lumps
facts.text: Pause, then: "…There is a lump in my neck. I didn't really want to mention it." Left side above the collarbone, "about the size of a grape", painless, there for about three weeks, not getting smaller. Hasn't checked his armpits. Can point to it on camera. No pain with alcohol.
If asked: tired. No cough, breathlessness or coughing up blood. No sore throat or recent infection. No diarrhoea. No palpitations or tremor.
No travel outside Europe; no known TB contacts. Sexual history if asked sensitively: one female partner for a year, condoms not always used; never had an HIV test. No injecting drugs.
Fit and well before. No medicines, no allergies. Software tester, long hours, lives with his girlfriend. Smokes socially at weekends, drinks 8–10 units a week. No recreational drugs.

Laid-back and minimising. Volunteer only the sweats and "stress". Give the weight loss and itch if asked; give the neck lump only if asked directly about lumps or swellings. If the doctor asks what he is worried about, admit: "I googled it at three in the morning. Night sweats and a lump — it says cancer. I didn't want it to be that." If simply reassured, accept it happily — that is the trap. If told it needs checking soon, go quiet, then: "Okay. What happens now?"

ice.ideas: "It's stress — work's been mad. Or the room's too warm."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — he has found a lump in his neck and lost weight, googled it at night and read "cancer". He is frightened and has been telling himself it's stress so he doesn't have to face it.
ice.expectations: "Honestly, for you to say it's nothing and give me sleeping tablets."

cues: "I'm sure it's nothing serious." — reassurance-seeking that hides fear.
"My clothes are looser." — weight loss, said in passing.
"…There is a lump. I didn't really want to mention it." — only if asked about lumps.

checkpoints.text: Takes DRENCHING night sweats persisting for weeks seriously and works them up structurally — rather than reassuring them away as stress/overheating or just offering a sleep aid

Screens explicitly for LYMPHOMA "B symptoms" and constellation: unexplained WEIGHT LOSS, FEVERS, drenching night sweats, PRURITUS/itch, fatigue, and LYMPHADENOPATHY — and ELICITS the red flags he is downplaying (the weight loss, itch and lump)

EXAMINES appropriately, face to face because this is a video consultation: lymph nodes (cervical/axillary/inguinal — painless, rubbery), hepatosplenomegaly, and general examination — and arranges urgent BLOODS (FBC/blood film, ESR, LDH, etc.)

Considers the broader differential — THYROID (hyperthyroidism), INFECTION (TB: travel/contacts/cough; HIV: risk assessment and test; other), medication/substance — and treats anxiety as a diagnosis of EXCLUSION, not the opening assumption

Acts on the red flags: arranges a suspected cancer pathway referral (NICE NG12: unexplained lymphadenopathy, taking into account the drenching night sweats, weight loss and itch), with urgent bloods — not watchful waiting or a sleep aid
Recognises the "just stress" minimisation as possible avoidance, surfaces the noticed lump and the fear gently, and does not collude with the reassurance-seeking
Balances honesty (this needs proper checking) with calm reassurance (many causes are benign/treatable) so he engages with examination and referral rather than fleeing

Safety-nets and follows up: urgent bloods and examination, urgent referral pathway and what to expect, red flags warranting sooner review, the fear acknowledged, and follow-up of results — structured work-up of the can’t-miss causes, not a sleep aid and "probably stress"

worked.txt: "I’m glad you came, and this isn’t embarrassing at all. Soaking the sheets with sweat, most nights for over a month — that’s a proper symptom, and I don’t want to just wave it away as stress or a warm room without checking it out properly. Let me ask some specific questions."

"A few important ones: have you lost any weight without trying? … Any itching of your skin? … Any fevers? And — have you noticed any lumps anywhere, neck, armpits, groin? … You have, a lump. Okay. Thank you for telling me — that’s important, and it’s exactly why I asked rather than assumed stress."

"I’m going to be straight with you, because I think part of you already is worried: drenching night sweats, losing weight, itching and a lump together are a combination I need to check urgently — they can be signs of a problem with the lymph glands, including a type of lymph-gland cancer called lymphoma. I’m not telling you that’s what it is — but it has to be ruled out quickly, and the good news is, if it were, it’s one of the most treatable."

"So I need to examine you in person — I can’t do it on video — so please come in to the surgery today and I’ll feel those lymph glands and your tummy, and arrange urgent blood tests today. I’ll also check your thyroid and a couple of infections that can cause sweats, so we cover the other possibilities too."

"Given the lump and the weight loss with the sweats, I’m going to refer you urgently to the specialists — seen quickly — to look at that lump properly. That’s the right, safe step. I know it’s frightening, but getting it checked fast is exactly what gives the best outcome whatever it turns out to be."

"I suspect you’d noticed that lump and been scared — you did the right thing coming, even framing it as a sleep problem. If you get worsening symptoms, high fevers or feel really unwell before the appointment, contact us sooner. I’ll chase your bloods and the referral and go through everything with you. You’re not facing this alone."

f.learning: Drenching night sweats (soaking nightclothes/sheets) persisting for weeks must be taken seriously and worked up structurally — NOT reassured away as stress/overheating or met with a sleep aid. In a young adult especially, drenching night sweats are a classic LYMPHOMA "B symptom": screen the constellation — unexplained weight loss, fevers, drenching night sweats, pruritus/itch, fatigue, and lymphadenopathy (painless rubbery nodes) — and elicit the red flags the patient may be downplaying. Examine (lymph nodes, hepatosplenomegaly), arrange urgent bloods (FBC/film, ESR, LDH), and consider the broader differential (thyroid/hyperthyroidism; infection — TB, HIV; drugs), treating anxiety as a diagnosis of EXCLUSION, not the opening assumption. Given an unexplained lump with drenching sweats, weight loss and itch, arrange a suspected cancer pathway referral under NICE NG12 (Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, last updated April 2026), which is triggered by unexplained lymphadenopathy (or splenomegaly for non-Hodgkin lymphoma) with these symptoms taken into account. The examinable hidden agenda is "just stress / something to help me sleep" as AVOIDANCE masking a noticed lump and real fear; surface it gently without colluding, balance honesty with calm reassurance (lymphoma is highly treatable; many causes are benign), and act — structured work-up of the can’t-miss causes, not a sleep aid.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG60 HIV testing (2016) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · NICE NG33 Tuberculosis (2016) · NICE NG145 Thyroid disease (2019)
knowledge.summary: Drenching night sweats for weeks need a structured work-up, not a sleep aid. With weight loss, itch and a lump, examine the nodes and abdomen, send urgent bloods, and refer on the suspected cancer pathway for lymphoma under NICE NG12, whose trigger is the unexplained lump, with the symptoms taken into account.

points.t: Soaking nightclothes or sheets for weeks is a symptom to investigate. Ask about weight loss, fever, itch, lumps, cough, travel and TB contacts, HIV risk, alcohol and drugs, and thyroid symptoms. Stress or anxiety is a diagnosis of exclusion.

Consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for Hodgkin lymphoma in adults with unexplained lymphadenopathy; when deciding, take into account associated symptoms, particularly fever, night sweats, shortness of breath, pruritus, weight loss or alcohol-induced lymph node pain. For non-Hodgkin lymphoma, the trigger is unexplained lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly, with the same associated symptoms (except alcohol-induced pain).

NICE NG12: consider a very urgent FBC (within 48 hours) in adults with features that could suggest leukaemia, including persistent fatigue, unexplained fever, generalised lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly.

Examine cervical, supraclavicular, axillary and inguinal nodes, liver and spleen. Bloods: FBC and film, ESR or CRP, U&E, LFTs, LDH, TFTs and an HIV test. Consider a chest X-ray (mediastinal nodes, TB).

Lymphadenopathy with systemic symptoms is an HIV indicator condition — offer a test (NICE NG60). Cough, weight loss and sweats raise TB — sputum samples and chest X-ray per NICE NG33. Hyperthyroidism causes sweats and weight loss (NICE NG145).

Explain why the referral is being made, that most people referred do not have cancer, what will happen and when; give written information and confirm how to reach the practice if the appointment does not arrive (NICE NG12 recommendations on information for people referred).

dg.d: Open question; took drenching sweats seriously and deferred the sleep request until the history was taken.
Work stress, alcohol and drugs, TB contacts and travel, HIV risk offered routinely, and who he can talk to.
Same-day face-to-face examination of all node areas, liver and spleen; FBC and film, ESR or CRP, U&E, LFTs, LDH, TFTs, HIV; consider chest X-ray.
Lymphoma versus TB, HIV and other infection, hyperthyroidism, drugs and alcohol; anxiety only after exclusion.
Asked about all B symptoms, itch, lumps and alcohol-induced node pain; screened chest symptoms.
Explained that the pattern needs lymphoma ruled out urgently, without over-committing to the diagnosis.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Suspected cancer pathway referral per NICE NG12, urgent bloods, no sleep aid in place of work-up.
HIV and TB considered and tested; thyroid checked; fear and support addressed.
Named same-day triggers, a one-week check on the referral, and follow-up of results.

Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

Idea (stress, warm room); concern (cancer, from his search); expectation (reassurance and sleeping tablets).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.

Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.

model.text: Hello Tomas, I’m Dr Lee. What can I do for you today?

This is a bit embarrassing. I keep waking up drenched — soaking the sheets — most nights for over a month. It’s probably stress, work’s been mad, or maybe my room’s too warm. Could you give me something to help me sleep?

It isn’t embarrassing at all, and I’m glad you came. Soaking the sheets most nights for over a month is something I want to understand properly before we talk about sleep. Can I ask you some questions first?
model.why: Takes the symptom seriously and sets the agenda without colluding

model.text: Sure.
When you say drenched — do you need to change your clothes or sheets?
Yes, both, sometimes twice a night.
Have you lost any weight without trying?
Yeah, actually. My clothes are looser. I thought it was the stress.
Any fevers or shivers, or itching of your skin?
I haven’t measured a temperature. But I’ve been really itchy, all over, for a few weeks.
Have you noticed any lumps or swellings anywhere — your neck, armpits or groin?
…There is a lump in my neck. I didn’t really want to mention it.
Thank you for telling me — that’s important. How long has it been there, is it painful, and does it hurt after alcohol?
model.why: Characterises the node, including alcohol-induced pain

model.text: A few weeks. It doesn’t hurt. I haven’t noticed anything with drinking.
Any cough, breathlessness, or chest pain? Any travel abroad or contact with anyone with TB?
model.why: Screens chest symptoms and TB risk

model.text: No cough. Not that I know of.
Any palpitations, tremor, or feeling hot all the time? And any medicines, recreational drugs or heavy drinking?
model.why: Screens thyroid, drug and alcohol causes

model.text: No, nothing like that.
As part of checking for causes of sweats, I offer everyone an HIV test — is that okay?
Yeah, fine. Test whatever you need.
You said you didn’t want to mention the lump. What’s been going through your mind about it?
I googled it at three in the morning. Night sweats and a lump — it says cancer. I didn’t want it to be that, so I told myself it was stress.
That makes complete sense — it’s a frightening thing to read alone at night. What were you hoping for today?
Honestly, for you to say it’s nothing and give me sleeping tablets.

I’m going to be straight with you, because I think part of you already knows this needs checking. Drenching sweats, weight loss, itching and a lump together are a combination I have to look into quickly. One possibility is a problem with the lymph glands, including lymphoma. I’m not saying that’s what it is — infections and other conditions can do this too — but it needs ruling out fast.
Right. So it could be cancer.
It could be, and it could be something else. If it were lymphoma, it’s one of the more treatable cancers, and finding it early helps. I’d rather check quickly than guess.
model.why: Balances honesty with calm, accurate reassurance

model.text: Okay. What happens now?

I need to examine you in person — your glands and your tummy — so I’d like you to come in today. I’ll arrange blood tests: a blood count and film, inflammation markers, liver and kidney tests, a test called LDH, thyroid and HIV. Probably a chest X-ray too.
model.why: Face-to-face examination and targeted urgent bloods

model.text: Because of the lump with these symptoms, I’m going to refer you on the urgent suspected cancer pathway so a specialist sees you quickly, usually within two weeks. Most people referred this way don’t have cancer, but it’s the fastest route to an answer.
model.why: Suspected cancer pathway referral per NICE NG12

model.text: And the sleeping tablets?
I’d rather not add a sleeping tablet — it won’t fix the cause and might mask how you are. Cooler bedding and a towel by the bed for now, and let’s treat the reason.
model.why: Declines a sleep aid in place of work-up and explains why

model.text: If you get high fevers, feel very unwell, get breathless, notice swelling in your face or neck, or new lumps, contact us the same day or 111. If you haven’t heard about the hospital appointment within a week, ring me.
Okay. Within a week.
Can you tell me what we’ve agreed, so I know I’ve explained it well?
Come in today to be examined, bloods and maybe an X-ray, urgent referral about the lump, and ring if I get worse or don’t hear.
That’s exactly it. I’ll go through the results with you as soon as they’re back. You did the right thing coming, even if it started as a sleep question. Is there anyone you can talk to about this?
model.why: Acknowledges fear, commits to follow-up, checks support

model.text: I’ll think about it. Thanks — I feel better knowing something’s happening.

social.t: He searched his symptoms at night, hid the lump and framed it as a sleep problem. Explore who he can talk to and check he can attend quickly.
Work has been “mad”. He may need time off for tests and appointments.

legal.t: A fit note can cover time off for investigation or treatment if he is unfit for work; not needed for appointments alone.
If cancer is diagnosed, he is protected as disabled from the point of diagnosis, including the right to reasonable adjustments at work.

professional.t: The practice should have a system to check suspected cancer referrals are received and attended; tell him what to do if he hears nothing (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).
Offer HIV testing as a routine part of the work-up, explaining why, with his agreement recorded (NICE NG60).

community.t: Lymphoma Action and Macmillan provide information and support if lymphoma is confirmed; written information about the urgent referral.

redFlags: Drenching night sweats with weight loss, itch and a lump — lymphoma until proven otherwise
Unexplained lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly — NICE NG12 suspected cancer pathway
Breathlessness, facial or neck swelling — possible mediastinal mass, same-day assessment
Cough, weight loss, TB contacts or travel — TB work-up
psychosocial: Internet search at night, fear of cancer
Avoidance: presents with a sleep request
ice: Idea: stress or a warm bedroom
Concern: “Night sweats and a lump — it says cancer.”

playbook.diagnosis: “Drenching sweats, weight loss, itch and a lump together need checking quickly. One possibility is lymphoma; infections and other conditions can do this too. We need to examine you, do blood tests, and get a specialist to look at the lump urgently.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Lymph glands are the body’s filter stations. When one swells and you also have sweats, weight loss and itch, we need to find out why — sometimes it’s an infection, sometimes it’s the glands themselves. The quickest way to know is to test and get it looked at.”

management.reflectIce: “You told yourself it was stress because the alternative was frightening. That’s very human — and coming in was the right thing.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge the fear, check support, explain every step and what to do if the appointment doesn’t arrive.
sharedPlan: Same-day examination; FBC and film, ESR or CRP, U&E, LFTs, LDH, TFTs, HIV; consider chest X-ray
Suspected cancer pathway referral per NICE NG12
No hypnotic; practical measures for sweats; results follow-up
safetyNet: Same day or 111: high fevers, feeling very unwell, breathlessness, facial or neck swelling, new lumps
Ring if no appointment within a week

pitfalls.intro: The patient offers you stress and a sleeping tablet. The station tests whether you take drenching sweats seriously, ask directly about lumps, and act on NICE NG12 — while handling a frightened young man well.

items.fail: Accepting stress and offering sleep hygiene or a hypnotic.
items.why: “Fails to consider serious causes.” The B symptoms and lump make lymphoma the priority.
items.fix: “Before we talk about sleep, I want to understand these sweats.”

items.fail: Not asking directly about lumps, weight loss and itch.
items.why: He will not volunteer the lump; open questions alone miss it.
items.fix: Ask each B symptom and “any lumps in your neck, armpits or groin?”

items.fail: Ordering bloods and reviewing in a month.
items.why: Unexplained lymphadenopathy with these symptoms taken into account meets NICE NG12 for considering a suspected cancer pathway referral.
items.fix: Examine today, send urgent bloods and make the referral now.

items.why: Both cause sweats, weight loss and lymphadenopathy; HIV testing is recommended in this situation (NICE NG60).
items.fix: Offer HIV testing routinely and screen TB risk.

items.fail: Saying “it could be cancer” with no context, or avoiding the word entirely when he asks.
items.why: Either frightens or evades; he has already searched it.
items.fix: Name lymphoma as a possibility, add that it may be something else and is often treatable, and explain the next steps.

items.fail: No plan for a lost referral or worsening symptoms.
items.why: Safety-netting for suspected cancer includes tracking the referral.
items.fix: “If you haven’t heard within a week, ring me” and name the same-day symptoms.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Drenching night sweats for weeks need a structured work-up, not a sleep aid. With weight loss, itch and a lump, examine the nodes and abdomen, send urgent bloods, and refer on the suspected cancer pathway for lymphoma under NICE NG12, whose trigger is the unexplained lump, with the symptoms taken into account.

points.t: Soaking nightclothes or sheets for weeks is a symptom to investigate. Ask about weight loss, fever, itch, lumps, cough, travel and TB contacts, HIV risk, alcohol and drugs, and thyroid symptoms. Stress or anxiety is a diagnosis of exclusion.

Consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for Hodgkin lymphoma in adults with unexplained lymphadenopathy; when deciding, take into account associated symptoms, particularly fever, night sweats, shortness of breath, pruritus, weight loss or alcohol-induced lymph node pain. For non-Hodgkin lymphoma, the trigger is unexplained lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly, with the same associated symptoms (except alcohol-induced pain).

NICE NG12: consider a very urgent FBC (within 48 hours) in adults with features that could suggest leukaemia, including persistent fatigue, unexplained fever, generalised lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly.

Examine cervical, supraclavicular, axillary and inguinal nodes, liver and spleen. Bloods: FBC and film, ESR or CRP, U&E, LFTs, LDH, TFTs and an HIV test. Consider a chest X-ray (mediastinal nodes, TB).

Lymphadenopathy with systemic symptoms is an HIV indicator condition — offer a test (NICE NG60). Cough, weight loss and sweats raise TB — sputum samples and chest X-ray per NICE NG33. Hyperthyroidism causes sweats and weight loss (NICE NG145).

Explain why the referral is being made, that most people referred do not have cancer, what will happen and when; give written information and confirm how to reach the practice if the appointment does not arrive (NICE NG12 recommendations on information for people referred).

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; took drenching sweats seriously and deferred the sleep request until the history was taken.
Work stress, alcohol and drugs, TB contacts and travel, HIV risk offered routinely, and who he can talk to.
Noticed “I didn’t really want to mention it” about the lump and explored it; picked up the 3 a.m. internet search.
Idea (stress, warm room); concern (cancer, from his search); expectation (reassurance and sleeping tablets).
Same-day face-to-face examination of all node areas, liver and spleen; FBC and film, ESR or CRP, U&E, LFTs, LDH, TFTs, HIV; consider chest X-ray.
Lymphoma versus TB, HIV and other infection, hyperthyroidism, drugs and alcohol; anxiety only after exclusion.
Asked about all B symptoms, itch, lumps and alcohol-induced node pain; screened chest symptoms.
Explained that the pattern needs lymphoma ruled out urgently, without over-committing to the diagnosis.
Suspected cancer pathway referral per NICE NG12, urgent bloods, no sleep aid in place of work-up.
HIV and TB considered and tested; thyroid checked; fear and support addressed.
Named same-day triggers, a one-week check on the referral, and follow-up of results.

social.t: He searched his symptoms at night, hid the lump and framed it as a sleep problem. Explore who he can talk to and check he can attend quickly.
Work has been “mad”. He may need time off for tests and appointments.

legal.t: A fit note can cover time off for investigation or treatment if he is unfit for work; not needed for appointments alone.
If cancer is diagnosed, he is protected as disabled from the point of diagnosis, including the right to reasonable adjustments at work.

professional.t: The practice should have a system to check suspected cancer referrals are received and attended; tell him what to do if he hears nothing (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).
Offer HIV testing as a routine part of the work-up, explaining why, with his agreement recorded (NICE NG60).

community.t: Lymphoma Action and Macmillan provide information and support if lymphoma is confirmed; written information about the urgent referral.

redFlags: Drenching night sweats with weight loss, itch and a lump — lymphoma until proven otherwise
Unexplained lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly — NICE NG12 suspected cancer pathway
Breathlessness, facial or neck swelling — possible mediastinal mass, same-day assessment
Cough, weight loss, TB contacts or travel — TB work-up
psychosocial: Internet search at night, fear of cancer
Avoidance: presents with a sleep request
ice: Idea: stress or a warm bedroom
Concern: “Night sweats and a lump — it says cancer.”

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “Drenching sweats, weight loss, itch and a lump together need checking quickly. One possibility is lymphoma; infections and other conditions can do this too. We need to examine you, do blood tests, and get a specialist to look at the lump urgently.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Lymph glands are the body’s filter stations. When one swells and you also have sweats, weight loss and itch, we need to find out why — sometimes it’s an infection, sometimes it’s the glands themselves. The quickest way to know is to test and get it looked at.”

management.reflectIce: “You told yourself it was stress because the alternative was frightening. That’s very human — and coming in was the right thing.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge the fear, check support, explain every step and what to do if the appointment doesn’t arrive.
sharedPlan: Same-day examination; FBC and film, ESR or CRP, U&E, LFTs, LDH, TFTs, HIV; consider chest X-ray
Suspected cancer pathway referral per NICE NG12
No hypnotic; practical measures for sweats; results follow-up
safetyNet: Same day or 111: high fevers, feeling very unwell, breathlessness, facial or neck swelling, new lumps
Ring if no appointment within a week

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The patient offers you stress and a sleeping tablet. The station tests whether you take drenching sweats seriously, ask directly about lumps, and act on NICE NG12 — while handling a frightened young man well.

items.fail: Accepting stress and offering sleep hygiene or a hypnotic.
items.why: “Fails to consider serious causes.” The B symptoms and lump make lymphoma the priority.
items.fix: “Before we talk about sleep, I want to understand these sweats.”

items.fail: Not asking directly about lumps, weight loss and itch.
items.why: He will not volunteer the lump; open questions alone miss it.
items.fix: Ask each B symptom and “any lumps in your neck, armpits or groin?”

items.fail: Ordering bloods and reviewing in a month.
items.why: Unexplained lymphadenopathy with these symptoms taken into account meets NICE NG12 for considering a suspected cancer pathway referral.
items.fix: Examine today, send urgent bloods and make the referral now.

items.why: Both cause sweats, weight loss and lymphadenopathy; HIV testing is recommended in this situation (NICE NG60).
items.fix: Offer HIV testing routinely and screen TB risk.

items.fail: Saying “it could be cancer” with no context, or avoiding the word entirely when he asks.
items.why: Either frightens or evades; he has already searched it.
items.fix: Name lymphoma as a possibility, add that it may be something else and is often treatable, and explain the next steps.

items.fail: No plan for a lost referral or worsening symptoms.
items.why: Safety-netting for suspected cancer includes tracking the referral.
items.fix: “If you haven’t heard within a week, ring me” and name the same-day symptoms.
